n: God tells Hosea to go again and love his wife, though she has been unfaithful—just as the Lord keeps loving Israel while they turn to other gods. Raisin cakes (KJV “flagons of wine”) were used in pagan festivals.

f.w: according to the love of the LORD toward the children of Israel

f.g: Better “cakes of raisins,” offered in Baal worship.

n: Hosea buys her back for fifteen shekels of silver plus barley—roughly the price of a slave. Gomer had apparently fallen into servitude, and Hosea pays to redeem her, a vivid picture of God redeeming His people at a cost.

f.g: About 6 bushels—barley was a cheap grain.

n: Hosea sets a period of waiting: she must stay with him faithfully, without other men, and he will be faithful to her. Restoration involves a time of discipline and rebuilding trust.

f.w: Thou shalt abide for me many days
f.g: A season of probation before full marital restoration.

n: Likewise, Israel will live a long time without king, sacrifice, or religious objects—both legitimate ones (ephod) and illegitimate ones (sacred pillars, household idols). This describes Israel’s long exile and scattering.

f.g: A sacred standing stone or pillar.
A priestly garment used to seek God’s will.

n: Afterward Israel will return and seek the Lord and “David their king”—the Messiah from David’s line—coming to Him with reverent awe in the latter days. Latter-day Saints see this fulfilled in the gathering of Israel to Christ.
